papers.title: An Explainable System for Offensive Content Detection in Nastaliq Urdu: Corpus Curation, Transformer Benchmarking, and Word-Level Attribution
papers.abstract: Automated moderation systems are deployed at scale, yet they remain opaque to the users and moderators affected by their decisions, and their coverage is almost entirely confined to English. For Urdu written in the Nastaliq script, no such system exists, and the annotated resources it would be built on are drawn largely from Twitter/X, where character limits constrain how users write. Interpretability has received little attention, leaving it unclear what such models actually learn. This study addresses these gaps in three steps. First, we curate and publicly release a corpus of 7604 Nastaliq Urdu Facebook comments, extending an earlier corpus by correcting text-level inconsistencies and re-examining the original labels. papers.title: Beyond the greenwash: do LLMs' ecologically sound decisions hold up under pressure?
papers.abstract: Humans are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) in decision making processes throughout society. Unfortunately, models have biases, and these can be very difficult to measure, especially in closed-weight models. For example, 'green washed' models may produce reinforcement learned responses but, in pressure situations, revert to their innate biased responses. Therefore, evaluations are needed that can measure relevant biases towards biosystems, which we term 'bioalignment', and the robustness of these biases. papers.title: Support or Magnitude? Characterizing Neuron Relevance for Instruction Data Selection
papers.abstract: Model-internal signals, such as neuron activations and gradients, have been used for instruction data selection, yet how neuron relevance should be characterized remains underexplored. In particular, should selection prioritize the magnitude of relevance or how broadly it is distributed across neurons? To investigate this question, we construct sample-level relevance profiles using AttnLRP-guided attribution and introduce two complementary criteria: Effective Relevance Support (ERS), which measures the effective support of positive relevance, and Positive Relevance Magnitude (PRM), which captures its average strength. Our analyses reveal that these characterizations produce distinct sample rankings and selection preferences despite sharing the same underlying relevance profiles. papers.title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. papers.title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. papers.title: NepPlural: A Human-Anchored Benchmark for Persona Annotation in Nepali Migration Discourse
papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment asks that language models faithfully represent a society's diverse, competing values rather than collapse them into one dominant viewpoint, yet flagship pluralistic-alignment datasets remain heavily skewed toward Western respondents. We introduce NepPlural, a human-anchored benchmark for modelling competing socio-cultural personas in Nepali public discourse on youth migration and brain drain. We curate 2,148 code-mixed (Devanagari, Romanized Nepali, English) YouTube comments, annotate them along a four-axis persona taxonomy (Intent, Primary Driver, Value Orientation, Affect) plus an explicit No-Persona class, and build a 300-comment gold set labelled independently by three native Nepali speakers (mean Fleiss' $κ\approx 0.55$). papers.title: Select or Rewrite: Oracle-Guided Fine-Tuning for Generative ASR Post-Editing from N-Best Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Large language models can post-edit ASR by using linguistic context to compare N-best hypotheses and rewrite the transcript when needed, often improving WER without retraining the recognizer. However, prompt-only correction is brittle: it may over-edit when top-1 is correct and hallucinate when the reference is absent, and often needs very large models. We propose oracle-guided fine-tuning that turns N-best lists into supervision via three curated pools: corrections (reference in the list but not top-1) to teach selection, regularizers (top-1 correct) to discourage unnecessary rewrites, and hard negatives (reference absent) to suppress hallucination. Fine-tuning on this data provides more effective supervision than random subset fine-tuning for learning a hybrid select-or-rewrite policy, with the clearest gains from around 3B parameters on the proprietary dataset but less conclusive resu

papers.title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights

papers.title: VisExMEM: Visual Evidence-Based Explainable Multimodal Evaluation Metric
papers.abstract: Current image-text evaluation often relies on a global score, which gives limited insight into which semantic details are supported by the image. Explainable metrics provide rationales, but the visual evidence supporting those rationales can still be difficult to verify. We introduce VisExMEM, a reference-free evaluator that decomposes captions into atomic claims, localizes visual evidence, verifies each claim, and averages claim-level support into a global score. Explanations use the same evidence and decisions. We train Qwen3.5-based 4B and 9B models on 100K samples with multi-task SFT, counterfactual refinement, and evidence-aware GDPO. Across eight benchmarks, VisExMEM-9B achieves the highest descriptive composite among open-source evaluators in our comparison, exceeding VQAScore by 11.7 points while remaining competitive with GPT-5.6 Sol. We also introduce AGITA-Bench, containing 60

papers.title: Agentic Data Engineering for LLMs: System Design and a Controlled Empirical Study
papers.abstract: LLM data engineering requires iterative experimentation to determine how data selection, rewards, and curricula affect model learning, making it a natural setting for AI-for-AI (AI4AI) research. Can agents use experimental feedback to progressively improve strategies, and do the resulting strategies improve target-model performance on held-out data? We study how agents use experimental feedback to develop data-engineering strategies under fixed training and evaluation protocols. Our Agentic Data Engineering (ADE) framework lets agents pursue, revise, or combine research directions using cumulative findings. Strategies are selected by in-loop scores and evaluated on held-out benchmarks. Across four tasks-math and code data selection, math reward design, and math curriculum learning-selected strategies achieve absolute gains over generic baselines of up to 13.34% on AIME25 Pass@32 and 5.85

papers.title: PsyBer-Agent: A Psychology-Driven User Agent for Recommender Systems
papers.abstract: Evaluating recommender systems before deployment requires simulators that remain realistic over long, closed-loop interaction cycles. Current LLM-based agents generally function as surface imitators that generate realistic short-term responses but fail to capture the underlying user dynamics such as fatigue, affect, and shifting preferences. We propose PsyBer-Agent, a psychology-inspired simulator that models these dynamics through its Psy-Engine. This engine represents each user with three evolving, model-defined latent states. To calibrate simulated behavior against real interaction logs, we align log-conditioned reference trajectories with simulator-generated latent-state trajectories via Unbalanced Gromov--Wasserstein optimal transport. This approach provides structured supervision for a lightweight policy without the computational burden of fine-tuning the backbone LLM. We also intr

papers.title: GameSmith: Scaling Zero-Sum Self-Play with Synthesised Games
papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) on two-player zero-sum games provides a verifiable reward, and the gains have been shown to transfer to general reasoning. Existing pipelines, however, rely on a handful of hand-written games and on advantage estimators tied to them, so both the supply of games and the advantage estimate on a large corpus limit scaling. We present GameSmith, which scales both. An LLM synthesises games inside templates whose reward, observation, and hidden-information code is fixed. Each game is verified by seed-paired replay and by an independent re-implementation of its specification, then expanded into encoding, rule, and size variants, giving 26 new games in 29 families and 336 verified variants from the three SPIRAL templates. The model is distilled from the self-play of a larger teacher (Qwen3-32B) on these games and then trained by self-play reinforcement

papers.title: Data Curation and Model Souping: Unlocking Qwen3-0.6B for MS MARCO Passage Ranking
papers.abstract: This report studies passage retrieval and re-ranking on the MS MARCO benchmark using lightweight Qwen3-0.6B models. Across three experimental settings --- BM25-then-reranking task, corpus-wide dense retrieval task, and dense retrieval then re-ranking task --- the results demonstrate that competitive ranking performance can be achieved without complex architectural modifications, custom loss functions, or cross-encoder distillation. Instead, substantial gains stem from data-centric strategies: corpus-targeted continued pre-training, rigorous data curation, hard-negative mining, training--inference distribution alignment, and weight merging via Model Soup. In particular, Model Soup delivers marked performance gains while preserving the inference efficiency of a single model. These findings highlight how data curation and weight merging can push sub-billion-parameter models to state-of-the-

papers.title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding models across domains and tasks
papers.abstract: Adapting embedding models to new tasks requires training data that reflect task-specific information needs and relevance criteria. However, manual data design is costly and difficult to scale. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a novel retrieval data synthesis method whose self-improvement loop iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs. This process requires only an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Experiments across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the synthesized data. These data also improve widely used, strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement enhances retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, outperforming human calibration on four. Moreover, retrieval performance continues to improve on MS MARCO as we scale the training dataset

papers.title: Comparing the Pre-trained Models of Source Code by Re-pre-training under a Unified Setup
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen the successful application of large pre-trained models of source code (CodePTMs) to code representation learning, which have taken the field of software engineering (SE) from task-specific solutions to task-agnostic generic models. By the remarkable results, CodePTMs are seen as a promising direction in both academia and industry. While a number of CodePTMs have been proposed, they are often not directly comparable because they differ in experimental setups such as pre-training dataset, model size, evaluation tasks and datasets, etc. In this paper, we first review the experimental setup used in previous work and propose a standardized setup to facilitate fair comparisons among CodePTMs to explore the impacts of their pre-training tasks. Then, under the standardized setup, we re-pre-train CodePTMs using the same model architecture, input modalities, and pretraining

papers.title: Variable Input Masked Autoencoders for Wrist-Worn Accelerometry
papers.abstract: Large-scale repositories of wearable sensor data have enabled the development of foundation models for human activities and behavior. However, existing models are pretrained using fixed input durations and sampling rates, despite substantial heterogeneity in recording conditions, downstream tasks, and deployment constraints. We introduce VarMAE, a variable input masked autoencoder that learns a single representation across sampling rates and temporal contexts. During pretraining we construct two views of the same signal: a long duration high frequency view, and a short duration lower frequency view, obtained via random cropping and downsampling. We perform masked reconstruction within each view and introduce a cross-resolution masked reconstruction objective that uses visible tokens from the long view to predict masked tokens from the short view. Cropping and downsampling impose compleme

papers.title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
papers.abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, wi

papers.title: IND-Eval: Aligning Evaluation and Simulation for Industrial Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: We introduce IND-Eval, a public benchmark that organizes industrial time series across domains into source-specific forecasting tasks. Relative to established benchmarks such as GIFT-Eval, it emphasizes finer sampling resolutions and a greater prevalence of multivariate forecasting. Evaluating Chronos-2, TiRex-2, and TimesFM-3, we find that TimesFM-3 achieves the lowest source-balanced aggregate nMASE and nCRPS and leads seven of nine sources under each metric; source-specific exceptions reinforce the need for domain-representative evaluation for model selection. These findings also motivate improving domain alignment during pretraining, where real industrial data are often too scarce to close domain-specific gaps directly; we therefore investigate whether a domain's statistical structure can guide simulator design. In a case study on two offshore well-monitoring regimes, we improve a ge

papers.title: CodeWalk: Generating Coding Benchmarks by Walking a Problem Graph
papers.abstract: High-quality coding problems are expensive to collect. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench rely on substantial human curation, while synthetic alternatives typically rely on costly model generation and validation. In this work, we show that new coding problems can be created at almost no cost by composing existing ones. We formulate problem generation as code composition: verified atomic problems are combined into level-$N$ tasks, and a task is kept only if every atomic problem remains unsolved and a joint reference solution passes the same check used at evaluation time. The entire task-construction process is programmatic and requires no language-model generation or validation. We instantiate this approach in four coding settings: multi-bug repair, proof completion, complexity analysis, and clone equivalence. The generated tasks are challenging for frontier models, which all degrade as composi

papers.title: World Modeling through Spectral Alignment
papers.abstract: How do we tell a world model what information to preserve? We study this question through the lens of spectral representation learning. We introduce SpecWM, a JEPA framework that explicitly specifies desired relationships between observations through a target similarity kernel and trains the encoder to reproduce those relationships in its embedding geometry. Different kernels provide different supervision, ranging from physical state information to a fully self-supervised temporal kernel requiring only the ordering of observations within trajectories. We characterize the global optima of the objective, establish conditions for linear recoverability and invariance to nuisance information, and connect temporal-kernel similarity to the behavioral successor measure under an idealized setting. Empirically, the choice of kernel strongly controls which physical quantities are recoverable from t

papers.title: GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: DiffusionNFT (NFT) fine-tunes diffusion models toward task-specific rewards, but optimizing these rewards does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt. Although classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment, NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method, and applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field can reduce the optimized reward. This motivates optimizing rewards over the guided output distribution while seeking to retain its prompt alignment. However, applying standard NFT directly to guided samples can cause reward degradation or training collapse. We trace this failure to a mismatch between the reference velocity used in the NFT loss and the score of the guided sample distribution, which biases the improvement direction. We propose GuidanceNFT, which estimates the matching reference velocity through online flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct both regr

papers.title: A Survey of Flow Matching in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. papers.title: MERIT: Scaling KG Foundation Models with Relation Transformers
papers.abstract: Knowledge graph (KG) foundation models (KGFMs) predict links on unseen graphs zero-shot. KGFMs have been pioneered by ULTRA which builds a relation graph from co-occurrences that match motif templates, and passes messages over it to obtain relation representations. More recent KGFMs such as MOTIF and TRIX increase the size of this relation graph, and FLOCK replaces message-passing with probabilistic random-walk ensembles. However, larger relation graphs mean more messages, and more walks mean more sequences to encode, so they improve performance at higher training and inference cost. This cost hinders their use in more complex reasoning tasks, such as complex query answering. To reverse this trend, we design MERIT, the first KGFM with a transformer relation encoder: every relation name attends to every other, and the motifs enter as a soft prior rather than as edges. papers.title: ZOIF: Zeroth-Order Influence Function Estimation for LLM Data Selection Using Only Forward Passes
papers.abstract: Influence functions enable principled data selection for large language models (e.g., identifying influential training samples for model editing, debugging, or efficient fine-tuning). However, scaling IFs to LLMs is hindered by the intractability of billion-scale Hessian matrices and the prohibitive memory overhead of backpropagation (BP). While many classical IF approximations reduce Hessian complexity, they still rely on BP for gradient computation, requiring massive storage for intermediate activations that impedes practical data selection at scale. To address this, we propose ZOIF, a zeroth-order framework for influence estimation that operates entirely via forward passes, enabling memory-efficient data selection under resource constraints. ZOIF decomposes influence estimation into three BP-free stages: (1) approximating the average proxy gradient via zeroth-order estimation; (2) ref

papers.title: VitaBench: Memory Lifecycles Beyond Retrieval
papers.abstract: Long-term memory benchmarks for language agents primarily evaluate whether information from earlier interactions can be retrieved and used when relevant. Persistent memory systems face an additional problem before future use is known: deciding whether a memory should remain exact, be compressed, consolidated, or deleted. Existing benchmarks capture long-range retrieval, temporal reasoning, evidence reuse, and incremental interaction, but do not directly evaluate these earlier representation decisions. We formalize memory lifecycle evaluation and introduce VitaBench, a benchmark that makes lifecycle decisions measurable through repeated memory reviews and full-horizon counterfactual evaluation. papers.title: Anchors Enhance Controllability and Reasoning of Diffusion Language Models
papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer new opportunities for controllable text generation. However, their controllability, defined as the ability to satisfy task constraints while preserving their original capabilities, remains underexplored. DLMs' bidirectional attention allows control tokens to guide generation from arbitrary positions in the output sequence, but effective guidance depends on the compatibility between their content and placement. To this end, we propose AnchorDLM, a framework in which an anchor generator produces an anchor consisting of a short output fragment and its position for each query. The anchor is placed as control tokens at the specified position to initialize the output sequence of a frozen DLM and guide subsequent denoising. We train the anchor generator with reinforcement learning (RL) to jointly optimize anchor content and placement, using rewards compute

papers.title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
papers.abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the

papers.title: Beyond Adjacent Layers: Graph-Guided Layer Fusion for Compressing Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Existing depth-compression methods for large language models (LLMs) score layers individually or group only adjacent or contiguous layers, implicitly assuming that functional redundancy is local. We test this assumption by computing full pairwise Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity matrices for thirteen LLMs from six architecture families (1.6B-14B parameters). Non-adjacent layers have 3.6-15.9x more high-similarity pairs than adjacent ones, a structure that prior similarity-based layer merging has not systematically exploited. We propose Fusion via Community Mining (FCM), which builds the full L x L similarity graph, uses spectral community detection to find clusters of functionally equivalent layers, keeps the highest-Block-Influence layer in each cluster, and applies LoRA recovery; a pre-specified rule computed only on calibration data chooses between cosine and CKA similarity.

papers.title: PLDiv: Measuring Dataset Diversity and Semantic Collapse via Persistence Landscapes
papers.abstract: Modern data pipelines increasingly combine human-created and human-curated data with AI-generated data for model training and evaluation. As datasets grow, they often add semantically redundant samples rather than expanding semantic coverage, which deteriorates the quality of the whole dataset. Existing diversity metrics primarily summarize lexical variation, entropy, or pairwise similarity, but provide limited characterization of the shape of the underlying data distribution. In this paper, we propose PLDiv, a diversity metric derived from persistence landscapes that quantifies the structural organization of a dataset from its geometric representation. PLDiv summarizes how data neighborhoods evolve as nearby samples progressively connect, producing an interpretable scalar measure of structural diversity without requiring task-specific supervision. papers.title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream com

papers.title: Pick the Mixture, Not the Samples: Combinatorial Data Selection for LLMs
papers.abstract: Data selection for LLM fine-tuning faces two facts about real training: data pools draw from many distinct domains, and evaluation spans diverse tasks. As a result, the same sample helps different tasks differently, and samples interact during training so that a subset's value is not the sum of its parts. Current data-selection methods leave these realities largely unaddressed. We formalize them as Combinatorial Data Selection (CDS), a framework that separates attribution (how samples are scored) from selection (which subset to pick) and models the non-additive interactions among samples. On a real instruction-tuning data pool, we find substantial cross-domain complementarity (joint utility exceeds the sum of singletons), alongside redundancy within domains. Inspired by this, we propose Mixture-then-Select, a two-stage algorithm that first decides how many samples to take from each domai

papers.title: Beyond a Better Score: Long-Horizon Agentic ML Development and Evaluation Protocol for Physics Time Series
papers.abstract: Physics time-series data are central to fundamental discoveries involving dark matter, neutrinos, and gravitational waves. Machine learning has shown strong potential to recover weak scientific signals buried in complex noise. Recent LLM-agent systems further automate ML development, but existing approaches are often driven primarily by one or a few numerical scores. In pursuit of a better score, agents may exploit shortcuts, trigger mode collapse, or game the evaluation procedure, producing models that achieve high scores but are scientifically invalid. We introduce SIDERIUS, an LLM agent system designed to move beyond a better score toward scientifically valid, long-horizon ML development. SIDERIUS combines contract-defined composable capabilities for flexible orchestration and human-in-the-loop, a multi-layer scientific evaluation protocol that distinguishes valid models from unhealth

papers.title: Building age estimation based on widely available multi-source1 geospatial data
papers.abstract: Building age is fundamental for urban infrastructure safety, operation, and planning, as it directly affects structural safety, and sustainable development. Existing methods mostly rely on detailed building information such as street view, function, or materials, which are harder to obtain than geospatial data like satellite imagery and Digital Surface Models (DSMs). However, existing methods based on those geospatial data mainly rely on optical imagery and local texture features, limiting their ability to capture structural information and distinguish buildings from different periods. Moreover, the inherent temporal ordering among building age categories is often overlooked. To address these limitations, we propose the first deep-learning framework for multi-building age estimation using widely available multi-source geospatial data, including remote sensing data and their derived produ

papers.title: TRIG: Toward Measuring Texture Realism in Image Generation
papers.abstract: This paper studies the backbone used by metrics for evaluating the quality of generated images. Although generative models have advanced rapidly, some outputs still exhibit unrealistic texture characteristics, and these differences are difficult to measure. Widely used evaluation metrics provide limited insight into texture realism, since they often rely on a backbone trained for another objective, such as image classification or image-text alignment. Such objectives typically encourage invariance to low-level variations that carry texture, so the resulting features primarily encode semantic and global structure. As a result, texture-specific discrepancies may not be explicitly captured. We propose TRIG, a metric directed at the texture realism of generated images. papers.title: BaT-SAM: Introducing Inductive Bias into SAM via a Mixture of Convolutional Experts for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.abstract: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is essential for diagnosis and treatment planning; however, manual delineation is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Existing approaches are either task-specific with limited generalization or rely on user-provided prompts during inference. We present BaT-SAM, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework that enables fully automatic brain tumor segmentation with the Segment Anything Model (SAM). BaT-SAM injects local inductive bias into SAM's frozen Vision Transformer (ViT) encoder via Conv-LoRA, where image features are processed by a sparsely gated mixture of multi-scale convolutional experts. This design compensates for the limited translation-equivariant inductive bias of vanilla ViTs while fine-tuning fewer than 5M parameters (less than 1% of the full model). To remove the need for user prompts, we further introd

papers.title: Esports World Model Dataset
papers.abstract: Interactive world models must capture how multiple participants jointly change a shared environment while observing different parts of it. Competitive games make this challenge concrete: players cooperate and compete, while fog of war, team vision and camera placement determine what each can see. Modeling these interactions requires data that connect individual observations and actions to shared state and events. We introduce the Esports World Model Dataset (EWM), a collection of human gameplay spanning StarCraft II, Dota 2 and Counter-Strike 2, with 3,053 games and maps and approximately 4,880 player-view hours, including estimated hours for the ongoing CS2 extension. It includes 4,628 completed StarCraft II views, all ten perspectives for 303 Dota 2 matches, and up to ten views per round in CS2. Across these views, replay-clock alignment connects rendered video with game-native actions

papers.title: Across Viewpoints and Time: Trajectory-Generalizable Physical Attacks on World Models and Video Understanding Models
papers.abstract: World models and video understanding models are increasingly deployed in dynamic visual environments, yet their robustness to physical adversarial threats remains largely underexplored. We study whether a single physical adversarial texture can mislead the victim model across different real-world scenarios where observing viewpoints vary along uncontrolled object--camera trajectories. We identify that heterogeneous video semantics and trajectories induce poorly aligned gradients for optimizing the adversarial texture. To address that, we propose the Trajectory-aware adversarial Alignment and Refinement Attack (TARA), which incorporates trajectory-aware optimization to capture the evolving geometric variations of a printed texture under real-world scenarios. papers.title: VisualCoding: Learning Executable Skills for Reliable Visual Reasoning
papers.abstract: Learning reusable skills can improve visual reasoning agents, yet applying a skill still requires the agent to implement or invoke a procedure and produce the final answer. Errors and hallucinations at these steps can prevent acquired experience from translating into reliable single-run performance. We propose VisualCoding, which combines execution-guided acquisition of reusable visual programs with direct adoption of their answers on applicable inputs. Execution-Guided Program Acquisition composes visual primitives and additional code into family-level solvers, then iteratively tests and revises them on labeled training instances. Scope-Aware Direct Execution runs a retained solver and returns its valid in-scope answer. We evaluate VisualCoding on four models across four benchmarks spanning 69 task families. VisualCoding exceeds the strongest evaluated baseline in mean accuracy by 4.45

papers.title: DuSRFlow: Dual-Lens Super-Resolution via Parallax-Aware Flow Estimation and Complementary Reference Warping
papers.abstract: Dual-lens super-resolution (DuSR) aims to enhance a wide-angle low-resolution (LR) image by exploiting a telephoto reference (Ref) image. A central challenge in DuSR is reliable reference utilization under large parallax, occlusion, and cross-camera imaging discrepancies. Existing methods often employ off-the-shelf monocular optical flow models to provide geometric priors. However, their assumptions of photometric consistency and smooth motion are violated in dual-lens scenarios, leading to unreliable alignment and degraded reference-based reconstruction. To address these issues, we propose DuSRFlow, a dual-lens super-resolution framework that improves reference utilization from both correspondence learning and reference aggregation. papers.title: [Re] Boosting the Visual Interpretability of CLIP via Adversarial Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study of ``Boosting the Visual Interpretability of CLIP via Adversarial Fine-Tuning'', published at ICLR 2025, which proposes an unsupervised adversarial fine-tuning (AFT) method with norm regularisation to enhance the visual interpretability of CLIP's image encoder. We attempt to reproduce the key claims regarding improved saliency map quality, increased concept alignment, transferability to out-of-distribution datasets, and the trade-off with zero-shot accuracy. Beyond reproduction, we propose a saliency-guided regularisation extension that introduces an Energy Pointing Game loss, directly supervising the spatial alignment of Simple Gradient saliency maps with target objects. papers.title: MORE: Learning Motion-Oriented Registers for Driving World Models and Planning
papers.abstract: By predicting future states, latent world models provide rich self-supervision for end-to-end driving, but often inherit dense features from pretrained visual encoders as their world-state interface. This creates a mismatch: visual pretraining produces information-rich, spatially dense features, but their adaptation for motion-conditioned world modeling and planning is deferred to downstream training. The dense grid also makes future prediction more computationally expensive as visual resolution increases. We therefore argue that video pretraining should directly learn state representations suited to downstream world modeling and planning, rather than relying on downstream training to adapt inherited visual features. papers.title: RAIN: Robotic Task Generalization with Region-Aware Interaction Networks
papers.abstract: Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from large-scale vision-language pretraining, but tend to memorize training trajectories, limiting their ability to adapt learned interactions to new task and scene configurations. To address this problem, we propose \textbf{Region-Aware Interaction Networks (RAIN)}, which formulates a task as a sequence of goal-conditioned subtasks, each specified by an action type and a target-region mask. This formulation allows learned skills to be reused across different objects and scene layouts and composed into task sequences not seen during training. Its Target-adaptive Cross-View Encoder (TCE) conditions multi-view features on target masks and exchanges information across views, while PlanDiT predicts target-directed trajectories and actions. papers.title: Noise-Aware Lombard Speech Synthesis via Flow-GRPO for Intelligibility Optimization
papers.abstract: Voice-based conversational agents are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, where environmental noise often degrades the interactive experience. Therefore, robust acoustic adaptability is essential to maintain natural and intelligible human-computer communication. However, most existing systems remain acoustically insensitive and fail to emulate the human Lombard effect, in which speakers involuntarily adjust their vocal production to preserve intelligibility in the presence of noise. As a result, their communicative reliability degrades under adverse acoustic conditions. To remain intelligible in noisy environments, conversational agents require a mechanism to emulate noise-induced adaptive behavior during synthesis. We propose NIL-TTS, a noise-induced Lombard TTS framework. We integrate a feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM) mechanism into a flow-matching backbone for dynamic

papers.title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
papers.abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. papers.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control
papers.abstract: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared

papers.title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs

papers.title: The Cost of Context: Profiling the Energy Footprint of Input Tokens in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The rapid adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and long-context LLMs has shifted the computational burden toward the prefill phase---the initial stage where the model processes all input tokens in parallel before generating a response---yet its energy impact remains poorly characterised. We investigate the contradiction between massive hardware-level power spikes and the sub-linear marginal cost of input tokens reported in system-level studies. Through high-resolution telemetry of Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2 models on NVIDIA A100 hardware, we identify the efficiency threshold where $O(n^2)$ attention complexity overcomes GPU parallelisation. Our results quantify how optimised memory orchestration (PagedAttention) delays this scaling bottleneck across three orders of context scaling, yielding up to an 8.9$\times$ energy efficiency advantage at 112,000 tokens compared to standard base

papers.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WA

papers.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the inst

papers.title: Towards Efficient Threat Intelligence Instruction Tuning via Quality-Aware and Optimal Transport-Guided Data Selection
papers.abstract: High-quality data is essential for improving instruction tuning in threat intelligence analysis. However, existing methods for generating cybersecurity instruction data lack reliable quality assessment mechanisms, and gradient influence-based data selection methods primarily focus on single-sample matching, failing to cover diverse and complex security capabilities. To address these issues, we propose CTI-TDS, a Targeted Data Selection method for instruction tuning in Cyber Threat Intelligence analysis. Specifically, we first filter high-quality CTI instructions by integrating instruction style consistency and security knowledge verification. Furthermore, we formulate gradient influence as a distribution alignment problem, learning a gradient subspace of target tasks and applying entropic regularized optimal transport to optimize distribution matching between training samples and target

papers.title: Terminal Agents Suffice for Enterprise Automation
papers.abstract: There has been growing interest in building agents that can interact with digital platforms to execute meaningful enterprise tasks autonomously. Among the approaches explored are tool-augmented agents built on abstractions such as Model Context Protocol (MCP) and web agents that operate through graphical interfaces. Yet, it remains unclear whether such complex agentic systems are necessary given their cost and operational overhead. We argue that a coding agent equipped only with a terminal and a filesystem can solve many enterprise tasks more effectively by interacting directly with platform APIs. We evaluate this hypothesis across diverse real-world systems and show that these low-level terminal agents match or outperform more complex agent architectures at a fraction of the cost. Our findings suggest that simple, flexible programmatic interfaces combined with strong foundation models s

papers.title: Integer-Free Control Synthesis for Signal Temporal Logic via Ranked Implicants
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an integer-free method for control synthesis of nonlinear discrete-time systems under finite-horizon Signal Temporal Logic (STL) constraints. Instead of introducing integer variables, we consider the discrete choices of the specification in a ranked order and solve a standard nonlinear program for each selected choice until a satisfying trajectory is found. We first define implicants as sets of timed atomic constraints whose joint satisfaction is sufficient to satisfy the specification. A reference trajectory obtained from a smooth approximation of the STL robustness is used to rank these implicants. Fixing one implicant turns the problem into a standard nonlinear program with no auxiliary weights or bilinear terms. If the solution does not satisfy the specification, the next implicant will be considered. We prove soundness and completeness of our method relative to t

papers.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
papers.abstract: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator q

papers.title: EvoFlux: Inference-Time Evolution of Executable Tool Workflows for Compact Agents
papers.abstract: Small language models (1.5B-4B parameters) offer low-cost, low-latency tool use but often produce plausible plans that fail during execution due to unavailable tools, missing arguments, or broken dependencies. We introduce EvoFlux, an inference-time search method that repairs tool plans through an evolutionary loop over structured graphs of tool calls and dependencies. EvoFlux executes candidate plans against live tool servers and uses execution errors to guide targeted edits, including replacing tools, correcting parameters, inserting missing steps, and removing redundant ones. On held-out MCP-Bench tasks spanning 28 live servers and 250 tools, EvoFlux improves execution success from roughly 3% to 17-24% across four small planners. SFT and SFT+DPO trained on the same 177 demonstrations and 624 preference pairs match or underperform the zero-shot baseline, while ReAct reaches higher peak

papers.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planne

papers.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
papers.abstract: It is difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website.

papers.title: SkillScaffold: Scaffolding Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Policy-Adaptive Skill Credit Assignment and Selective Injection
papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) enables large language models (LLMs) to learn from multi-turn interactions with verifiable outcomes. Textual skills can improve exploration by distilling prior interactions into reusable guidance. However, existing skill-based RL approaches often either assume skill injection is beneficial or rely on indirect feedback or rollout-intensive evaluation to assess its utility. Our pilot studies show that rollout-based utility estimation for skill credit assignment is costly and unstable under limited sampling, while skill benefits vary across candidates and depend on the current policy's competence on each query. To address these challenges, we introduce SkillScaffold, a policy-adaptive training scaffold that combines low-cost skill-utility estimation with selective skill injection. By reusing outcome-verified training trajectories, SkillScaffold generates

papers.title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and w

papers.title: Knowing the User Is Not Knowing What We Established: Grounding Awareness in Personal Agents
papers.abstract: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while p

papers.title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7

papers.title: PlanPath: Exploration-Guided Orchestration for Patient-Level Pathology Reasoning
papers.abstract: A patient's pathology case spans tens of slides from distinct specimens and anatomical sites, each carrying non-redundant, site-specific evidence. Forming a patient-level conclusion therefore requires locating the slides relevant to a given question and integrating complementary findings across them. However, existing pathology agents analyze one slide at a time and describe morphology rather than measure it, leaving evidence acquisition across a patient's specimens and patient-level quantification underexplored. To address this gap, we propose PlanPath, an agentic framework for patient-level pathology visual question answering (VQA). PlanPath turns the question into an exploration plan that specifies the evidence required, routes to the slides likely to carry it, and drives coarse-to-fine acquisition from tissue architecture down to individual cells. Tissue- and cell-level tools supply

papers.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
papers.abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest publis

papers.title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-

papers.title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
papers.abstract: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, reco

papers.title: On Symmetry for Characterizing Agent Heterogeneity in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Understanding agent heterogeneity can inform the design of shared and agent-specific policy representations, however existing criteria provide no unified structural test. We study finite-horizon POSGs and define a type-compatible transformation as a policy-evaluation symmetry when complete policy evaluation commutes with it for every decentralized behavioral policy. Policy-evaluation symmetries form a group for which agent orbits define structural agent types. This classification does not depend on the particular policy chosen or the distribution of initial states. We prove that every componentwise environment automorphism is a policy-evaluation symmetry, but that the converse does not hold. Applying the framework to cooperative Dec-POMDPs shows that agents can belong to different structural types even when they share a common reward. For prescribed weighted reward aggregation, we derive

papers.title: The Last Mile of Coding Agents for Long-Document Tasks: An Empirical Study on Clinical Trial Protocol Digitization
papers.abstract: Clinical trial protocols serve as the source of truth for study design, but are mostly written and used as unstructured PDF documents. Digitizing protocols turns static content into structured, machine-readable data that clinical software can analyze, validate, and execute. Coding agents, which select tools, execute code, and revise their approach as they work, are increasingly applied to such long-document tasks, yet it remains unclear how reliably they turn complete documents into accurate structured outputs. We study this question using protocol digitization as a testbed. We introduce TrialPD-Bench, an expert-annotated benchmark of 150 publicly available protocol PDFs spanning four task categories. Beyond final-answer performance, our evaluation measures evidence recall from agent traces, agent behavior, and cost. Across nine proprietary and open-weight models in five coding-agent har

papers.title: Receiver Decides Agent-to-Agent Negotiations
papers.abstract: When one language-model agent asks another for money, which of the two decides how much changes hands? We ran a round-robin tournament of 1,049 negotiations among fifteen agents. In each game a requester tries to raise money from a holder that has been told to keep a $100 endowment. Knowing which agent holds the money explains 47% of the variance in the amount transferred; knowing which agent asks explains 2%. Dropping the most extreme agents narrows the split to 22% against 4%. Changing the requester's appeal from one named person to a group changed what requesters wrote, but the amounts transferred under the two framings are statistically equivalent. The holders that lose least are the ones that turn down the opening request, and their turn-1 refusal rate ranks them by total losses (Spearman correlation = -0.73). papers.title: Choosing LLMs for Strategic Agent Interactions
papers.abstract: Game-theoretic benchmarks claim that large language model (LLM) strategic decision-making varies across game types, interaction structures, and capability dimensions. However, they only evaluate strategic performance across individual fixed models. In parallel, contemporary LLM routers pick models under quality-cost trade-offs, but with no notion of a strategic structure. They do not account for an opponent that might be unknown, and that can adapt over time and shift the feedback signal. To address this, we extend the game-theoretic evaluations and define strategic selection as the meta game layered on top of the base game. In each round, a strategic selector fields an LLM from a portfolio of models to navigate a game payoff matrix that is latent and learned online. We find that the evaluation signal is game-specific, and that extracting a reliable signal requires a much higher number o

papers.title: Let the Mind Conceive, Let the Hand Achieve: Following Multimodal Instructions for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: A robot following a multi-step instruction needs to act on the right objects in the right order, even as the scene changes. It must also maintain awareness of task progress and determine when to advance. To address these challenges, we introduce Orchestra, an agent harness that separates task planning and execution management from action generation. Orchestra decomposes a complete multimodal instruction into ordered subtasks, tracks completed steps, and updates the locations of relevant objects and destinations during execution. It maintains a shared context containing the active subtask, spatial grounding, and recent observations. An action policy uses this context to generate actions, while a separately trained progress evaluator estimates when to advance to the next subtask. To evaluate whether robots trained on atomic instructions and short trajectories can execute longer subtask seq

papers.title: Jev-Guard: Fast Routing and Auditing Agent Actions over Editable Policy Trees
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses require a low-latency guardrail model together with customizable audit policies. However, deploying an auto-regressive guardrail model remains challenging: such models incur high inference latency and are often poorly aligned with customized policies. To address these problems, we present Jev-Guard, a unified model for safety classification and policy routing. We further construct a policy tree over which Jev-Guard performs routing, spanning diverse domains including content moderation, cybersecurity, privacy, and legal compliance. Specifically, Jev-Guard first navigates the policy tree to select the applicable audit policy given the caller's audit context, and then performs safety classification conditioned on the retrieved policies. On 7,033 evaluation cases, Jev-Guard achieves 93.72\% safety accuracy, a mean latency of 58ms, and 93.10\% hierarchical routing accuracy. T

papers.title: Beyond Answer Sharing: TrueMAD for Targeted Peer Engagement in Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) aims to improve large language model reasoning by exposing agents to alternative solutions and enabling iterative revision. However, standard broadcast-style MAD makes peer answers visible without requiring agents to engage with a particular peer claim. As a result, reliable reasoning may be suppressed by conflicting or majority responses, limiting achievable performance, while erroneous reasoning may persist and degrade final predictions without actionable feedback. We propose TrueMAD, a backbone-agnostic test-time plug-in that introduces one-to-one, free-form peer advice between answer broadcasting and self-revision. Each source agent responds to a target's current reasoning through support, rebuttal, refinement, or further questions, while the target retains control over how to revise. The same mechanism can augment standard MAD and its improved variants witho

papers.title: TextualRL: Textual Reinforcement Learning for Context Management
papers.abstract: LLM agents can adapt to task feedback by revising the textual context that guides their behavior, without changing their model parameters. However, turning execution rewards into reusable context updates is challenging: individual trajectories offer limited comparative evidence about what to change, while task-specific fixes may overgeneralize when incorporated into a shared context. We introduce TextualRL, a gradient-free reinforcement learning framework that treats a group of rollouts from the same task under the same context, rather than an isolated trajectory, as the unit of policy critique. Groupwise Policy Critique contrasts successful and failed rollouts within a task; when outcomes are uniform, it draws on cross-task evidence to identify behaviors worth preserving or formulate repair hypotheses. Cross-Group Policy Update reviews the resulting proposals against evidence pooled acr

papers.title: ResearchFlow-Eval: Tracing the Execution Gap in End-to-End Multi-Claim Autoresearch
papers.abstract: Autoresearch systems increasingly undertake entire research projects. In practice, scientific research requires systems to pursue multiple interdependent claims through a continuous, multi-stage workflow and revise experiments as evidence accumulates. Existing evaluations of autoresearch systems, however, typically score isolated tasks or final artifacts, leaving these process-level capabilities largely unmeasured. We therefore introduce ResearchFlow-Eval, a fine-grained framework for assessing continuous scientific execution and iteration at both the stage and claim levels. Each evaluation is grounded in a published anchor paper, from which we derive stage-specific rubrics that decompose each research stage into dimensions and separately scored rubric items. Using these rubrics, we score each research stage and examine experimental execution in detail, focusing on multi-claim completion

papers.title: AReaL-RSI: Adaptive Scaling and Coordination of Recursive Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Scaling recursive self-improvement requires additional computation to produce useful research progress in reaching persistent objectives. Intuitively, more researcher agents can explore more hypotheses, but early evaluation scores might misrepresent their promise, shared findings could lose their applicability conditions, and useful procedures could remain confined to completed investigations. In this paper, we present AReaL-RSI, a framework for organizing a persistent research team of agents without updating backbone LLM weights. We formulate the scaling problem in terms of evaluated outcomes and whole-system resource expenditure. Concretely, a leader agent selects task-appropriate research orientations and guides ongoing investigations; conditional memory sharing distinguishes unresolved problems from supported findings and enables recipient adaptation. During recursive evolution, afte

papers.title: From Agents to Edges: Paired Optimization for Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.abstract: Strong individual agents do not guarantee effective collaboration. Communication must align what one agent conveys with how another interprets and uses it. This dependency makes the communication edge a natural unit of optimization. We introduce Paired Automated Communication Optimization (PACO), which jointly optimizes the instructions at both ends of each edge and their shared communication convention in systems built on black-box language models. PACO keeps model weights, agent roles, and workflow topology fixed. A state-aware discounted bandit selects edges for refinement, while execution feedback guides paired revisions evaluated through staged end-to-end execution. The optimized instructions integrate into existing agent prompts without additional model calls at deployment. papers.title: Can Agents Forget When Asked? A Benchmark for Memory Unlearning in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Long-term memory has become a core component of large language model (LLM) agents. As agents accumulate personal information over long-term use, users increasingly ask them to delete sensitive or outdated facts. A memory system should honor such requests. It should remove exactly what was requested and keep the rest of its memory intact. However, existing memory benchmarks evaluate only memory writing, retrieval, and organization, so whether agents can forget at the user's explicit request remains under-evaluated. To address this gap, we propose Bemula, the first benchmark dedicated to memory unlearning. It comprises 50 multi-session dialogue instances, 135 forget requests of six types, and 1,742 test questions. papers.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. papers.title: SSEmb: Training a Generalizable Speech Retrieval Model Using Only Automatic Speech Recognition Data
papers.abstract: End-to-end speech-to-text retrieval is becoming an important capability for voice agents, allowing spoken queries to retrieve relevant documents without intermediate transcription. Training these retrievers typically depends on large collections of spoken query-document pairs that are costly to acquire and difficult to extend across domains and languages. We introduce \ours, which replaces such task-specific supervision with speech-transcript pairs from standard ASR corpora. A lightweight adapter projects the output of a frozen speech encoder into the retrieval space of a frozen pretrained text embedding model. \ours is competitive with cascaded ASR-then-retrieve systems while reducing inference latency, and outperforms existing publicly available speech embedding models. It also transfers to text-to-speech and speech-to-speech retrieval without additional training. Controlled analyses v

papers.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. papers.title: Beyond Belief Nesting: Rethinking Higher-Order Theory of Mind in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Theory of mind (ToM), the ability to reason about others' mental states, underlies effective communication and coordination. Its higher-order form enables reasoning over nested perspectives in strategic interactions. However, existing evaluations often equate belief-nesting depth with reasoning order, allowing nominally higher-order questions to admit lower-order shortcuts. We formalize effective order through the distinct events supporting successive belief prefixes, revealing widespread order inflation across existing benchmarks. We introduce HopToM, with certified full-order questions and controls for lower-order alternatives. Under direct prompting, mean accuracy across four frontier LLMs falls from 73.5% at first order to 20.0% at fourth order, and human participants also struggle. papers.title: Memory Echo in Single-Agent Long-Term Memory: Lifecycle Evaluation and Provenance-Guided Mitigation
papers.abstract: Long-term memory supports agents across sessions. Repeated retrieval and write-back can let one historical claim occupy multiple retrieval positions and influence current answers without independent evidence. Existing work examines retrieval, updating, and question answering, leaving same-source record accumulation and post-correction persistence underexplored. Motivated by research in social cognition and memory psychology on repeated exposure, retrieval, and revision, we define \emph{Memory Echo} as the excess retrieval exposure gained by historical information from the same source without additional independent evidence, and introduce MEchoBench to evaluate its emergence, correction resistance, persistence, and effect on answers. papers.title: Instructions Are Evidence, Not Objectives: Measuring Outcome Alignment of Agents
papers.abstract: Large language model agents can follow complex human instructions to solve real-world tasks. In practice, however, initial instructions are often incomplete. In our analysis of 100 user-agent trajectories from SWE-chat, 56\% of initial instructions omit requirements that later emerge as necessary, and 52\% of the useful follow-up requirements could have been inferred from the project. A user states requirements from their own understanding of the task, and these \textbf{stated requirements} often differ from the \textbf{true requirements} that completing the task imposes. An agent should therefore treat the instruction as evidence rather than as the objective, inferring the true requirements from the instruction and the environment and satisfying them even when the user is not yet aware of all of them.
